title: One Word Substitution
summary: A phrase such as 'murder of a king' must be replaced by one word (regicide). Options are built from suffix families —cide, -phobia, -logy, -cracy, -phile — so classifying the family first kills half the options. The bank below carries 150+ exam-frequency substitutions grouped for daily revision.

subtopics.title: Suffix families: decode the word by its ending
subtopics.concept:
One-word-substitution items rarely need a giant dictionary — the ending of the answer already tells you its *family*, and options are built one per family. Learn the suffix, and every member of the family is within reach.

**-cide — the act of killing**

• Regicide – killing a king
• Genocide – killing a whole race or community
• Fratricide – killing one's own brother
• Infanticide – killing an infant
• Patricide – killing one's father
• Suicide – killing oneself
• Homicide – killing a human being
• Sororicide – killing one's sister

**-phobia — an abnormal fear of**

• Hydrophobia – fear of water
• Claustrophobia – fear of confined spaces
• Acrophobia – fear of heights
• Xenophobia – fear or dislike of foreigners
• Nyctophobia – fear of darkness
• Haematophobia – fear of blood
• Triskaidekaphobia – fear of the number thirteen
• Photophobia – abnormal sensitivity to light

**-ology — the study of**

• Anthropology – study of humankind's development
• Ornithology – study of birds
• Entomology – study of insects
• Zoology – study of animals
• Philology – study of languages and their history
• Etymology – study of word origins
• Geology – study of the earth's rocks
• Psychology – study of the mind
• Sociology – study of society
• Seismology – study of earthquakes

**-graphy / -grapher — writing/recording, or its practitioner**

• Geography – study of the earth's surface
• Demography – statistical study of populations
• Calligraphy – the art of fine handwriting
• Cartography – the making of maps
• Hagiography – writing of saints' lives
• Lexicographer – one who compiles dictionaries

**-cracy / -crat — rule or power**

• Democracy – government by the people
• Autocracy – rule by one absolute ruler
• Bureaucracy – government by paid officials
• Aristocracy – rule by the noble class
• Theocracy – rule in the name of God
• Plutocracy – rule by the wealthy
• Mobocracy – rule by the mob
• Meritocracy – rule by ability and merit

**-phile / -phile words — one who loves**

• Bibliophile – a lover of books
• Philatelist – a lover and collector of stamps
• Anglophile – a lover of England or English ways
• Philanthropist – one who loves humankind through charity

**-vore / -phagous — feeding on**

• Carnivorous – flesh-eating
• Herbivorous – plant-eating
• Insectivorous – insect-eating
• Omnivorous – eating everything

**-gamy / -gamy words — marriage patterns**

• Monogamy – marriage to one person at a time
• Polygamy – marriage to several spouses
• Bigamy – marrying while legally married to another
• Exogamy – marriage outside one's own group

**How the family method wins.** The stem 'murder of a king' invites four options, usually one -cide word, one -ology word, one -phobia word, one person-word. Knowing -cide = killing filters to the candidates, and then plain sense (rex = king → regicide) finishes. You never needed to memorise 'regicide' as a whole.

**Stack two families for rare words.** *Nyctophobia* = nycto (night) + phobia (fear) → fear of darkness. *Entomology* = entomo (insect) + logy (study). Rare SSC words are nearly always transparent stacks — the examiner picks words that reward this decoding.

**TheGreek/Latin counting prefixes** multiply coverage: mono (one), bi/duo (two), tri (three), quad (four), poly (many), pan (all), omni (all), semi (half), hemi (half), cent (hundred), milli (thousand). *Omnipotent/omniscient/omnipresent* are one prefix + one root each.

tricks.title: Family filter
tricks.body: Classify the stem first: is it a killing word, a fear, a study, a ruler-system, a person-type, a place? Reject every option from a different family before reading further.

example.q: Murder of a king: homicide / regicide / ornithology / hydrophobia.
example.solution: Killing stem → -cide family only → regicide (rex/reg = king). Homicide kills 'a human' generally — the specific stem wins.

tricks.title: Root + suffix stack
tricks.body: Split rare answers: nycto-phobia, entomo-logy, carto-grapher. Two known parts beat one memorised word.

tricks.title: Counting-prefix drill
tricks.body: One evening per prefix set: mono-, bi-, tri-, poly-, pan-, omni-. Write each with three familiar words and the family stays for life.

mistakes: Confusing fratricide (brother) with patricide (father) — the family root carries the relation.
Mixing -phobia (fear) with -phile (love) under exam pressure.
Choosing astrology for a 'scientific study of stars' stem — astronomy is the science, astrology the belief system.
Memorising isolated words instead of suffix families; the family is what survives pressure.

subtopics.title: One word for people: traits, trades and types
subtopics.concept:
The largest OWS category names a *person by what they do, feel or suffer*. Four sub-buckets organise the bank:

**1. Trades and professions** (learn with the tool or object of the trade): cobbler–shoes, plumber–pipes, cartographer–maps, lexicographer–dictionaries, obstetrician–childbirth, astronomer–stars (science), astrologer–stars (prediction).

**2. Character and conduct:** miser (hoards money), spendthrift (wastes it), teetotaller (never drinks), glutton (overeats), garrulous (overtalkative), taciturn (speaks little), gullible (believes easily), sceptic (doubts), novice (beginner), veteran (long-experienced).

**3. Loyalty and betrayal:** patriot/traitor, martyr (dies for a cause), apostate (abandons his religion), vandal (destroys property for pleasure), firebrand (stirs up unrest).

**4. Omnipotence set:** omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing), omnipresent (present everywhere) — three words, one prefix, endlessly reused.

**People bank (revise in five-word batches)**

| One-word substitution | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **One who talks in sleep** | Somniloquist |
| **One who walks in sleep** | Somnambulist |
| **One who cannot read or write** | Illiterate |
| **One who knows many languages** | Polyglot |
| **One who lives shut off from the world** | Recluse (or Hermit) |
| **One who spends beyond his means to impress** | Extravagant (a spendthrift) |
| **One who is extremely careful with money** | Miser |
| **One who never drinks alcohol** | Teetotaller |
| **One who deals in cattle** | Drover |
| **One who mends shoes** | Cobbler |
| **One who cuts and sells men's clothing** | Tailor (a men's outfitter) |
| **One who sells medicines and prepares them** | Pharmacist (or Chemist) |
| **One who performs surgical operations** | Surgeon |
| **One who fits and repairs water pipes** | Plumber |
| **One who makes maps** | Cartographer |
| **One who compiles a dictionary** | Lexicographer |
| **One who writes the life history of another** | Biographer |
| **One who writes his own life story** | Autobiographer |
| **One who studies the human mind** | Psychologist |
| **One who treats eye disorders** | Oculist (or Optometrist) |
| **One who treats teeth** | Dentist |
| **One who foretells events by the stars** | Astrologer |
| **One who studies the stars scientifically** | Astronomer |
| **One who travels in space** | Astronaut (or Cosmonaut) |
| **One who is new to a profession** | Novice (or Tyro) |
| **One who has long experience of a field** | Veteran |
| **A person appointed to hear and decide a dispute** | Arbitrator |
| **One who deliberately damages property** | Vandal |
| **One who incites others to violence** | Firebrand |
| **A person who loves his country deeply** | Patriot |
| **One who betrays his country** | Traitor |
| **A person of great courage** | Valiant (a gallant) |
| **One unable to speak** | Dumb (speech-impaired) |
| **One unable to hear** | Deaf |
| **One who is present everywhere** | Omnipresent |
| **One who knows everything** | Omniscient |
| **One with unlimited power** | Omnipotent |
| **A woman whose husband has died** | Widow |
| **A man whose wife has died** | Widower |
| **One who has just been married** | Newly-wed (bride/groom) |
| **One who eats too much** | Glutton |
| **One who talks too much** | Garrulous (or Loquacious) |
| **One who speaks little** | Taciturn (or Reserved) |
| **One who believes everything easily** | Gullible |
| **One who doubts everything** | Sceptic |
| **One who hates humankind** | Misanthrope |
| **One who sacrifices life for a cause** | Martyr |
| **One who deserts his religion** | Apostate |
| **One who avoids company and merriment** | Introvert (a recluse) |
| **One who shows off his learning** | Pedant |

**Sensory and status pairs** are quick marks: dumb/speech-impaired, deaf, widow/widower, newly-wed. Note the gender-symmetric pairs — SSC loves the widow/widower switch under time pressure.

tricks.title: Object-anchor the trade
tricks.body: Never learn 'cobbler' alone — learn 'cobbler → shoes'. Stems name the object ('one who repairs shoes'), and your anchor matches it instantly.

tricks.title: Contrast pairs together
tricks.body: Store opposites and neighbours in one card: garrulous ↔ taciturn; miser ↔ spendthrift; novice ↔ veteran. The stem often points to one side of a pair.

tricks.title: Omni-triplet
tricks.body: One prefix (omni- = all), three endings: -potent (power), -scient (knowing), -present (place). One card covers all three SSC favourites.

mistakes: Swapping astrologer and astronomer — decide by 'scientific' or 'prediction' in the stem.
Using 'mediator' where the stem demands an authorised decider — arbitrator decides, a mediator facilitates.
Mixing spendthrift (wastes) with miser (hoards).
Answering with an adjective when the stem's pattern expects the person-word.

subtopics.title: One word for places and groups
subtopics.concept:
**Places.** The stem pattern is 'a place where X is kept/stored/done'. Anchor each place to its stored object:

**Places bank**

| One-word substitution | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A place where bees are kept** | Apiary |
| **A place where birds are kept** | Aviary |
| **A place where fish are kept** | Aquarium |
| **A place where grains are stored** | Granary |
| **A place where horses are kept** | Stable |
| **A place where money is coined** | Mint |
| **A place where weapons are stored** | Armoury |
| **A place where dead bodies are kept** | Mortuary |
| **A place where orphans live** | Orphanage |
| **A place where historical objects are displayed** | Museum |
| **A place where aircraft are kept and repaired** | Hangar |
| **A place where novels, poems etc. are produced** | Publishing house (or Press) |
| **A place for public speaking and debate** | Podium (the speaker's platform) |
| **A burial place outside a church** | Cemetery |
| **A place where monks live together** | Monastery |
| **A place where nuns live together** | Convent |
| **A building where goods are made by hand or machine** | Factory (or Workshop) |
| **A place where animals are slaughtered** | Abattoir |

Watch the near-pairs: *apiary* (bees) vs *aviary* (birds) differ by one letter; *granary* (grain) vs *granite* (rock) — the exam plants exactly these neighbours as options.

**Groups (collective nouns).** The stem pattern is 'a group of X':

**Groups bank**

| One-word substitution | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A group of lions** | Pride |
| **A group of wolves** | Pack |
| **A group of bees** | Swarm |
| **A group of sheep** | Flock |
| **A group of cattle** | Herd |
| **A group of fish** | School (or Shoal) |
| **A group of stars forming a pattern** | Constellation |
| **A group of islands** | Archipelago |
| **A group of skilled judges or experts** | Panel |
| **A group of worshippers** | Congregation |
| **A group of musicians playing together** | Orchestra (or Band) |
| **A group of soldiers** | Troop (or Platoon) |
| **A group of ships sailing together** | Fleet |
| **A group of hairs growing together** | Tuft |

Collective nouns are pure memorisation but tiny in number — twenty cover nearly every paper. Note the precision points: lions come in a *pride* (not a herd), wolves in a *pack*, fish in a *school*, islands in an *archipelago* (not a chain of villages!).

**Choosing between group options** is a one-letter game under pressure: swarm (bees/insects), flock (sheep/birds), herd (cattle), pride (lions), pack (wolves/dogs). Ask which animal the stem names before touching the options.

tricks.title: Stored-object anchor
tricks.body: Places are defined by what is inside: bees→apiary, birds→aviary, grain→granary, coins→mint, corpses→mortuary. Match the object, not the sound.

example.q: A place where bees are kept: aviary / apiary / aquarium / granary.
example.solution: Bees → **apiary**. 'Aviary' differs by one letter — the deliberate neighbour-trap.

tricks.title: Animal-first matching
tricks.body: For group stems, name the animal first, then recall its partner noun. Options scramble the five common pairs; the animal decides.

tricks.title: Near-pair cards
tricks.body: Make cards for one-letter pairs: apiary/aviary, granary/granite, monastery/convent (men/women). These are where marks leak.

mistakes: Choosing 'aviary' for bees (one-letter trap).
Calling a lion group a 'herd' — lions take 'pride'.
Confusing monastery (men) and convent (women).
Using 'army' for a group of soldiers in the collective-noun sense when the stem wants 'troop/platoon'.

subtopics.title: Government systems, studies and word-craft
subtopics.concept:
**Government by whom?** The stem always names the ruler — match the ruler to the suffix -cracy or the classical root:

- by the **people** → democracy; by **officials** → bureaucracy; by the **rich** → plutocracy; by the **nobles** → aristocracy; by **God/clergy** → theocracy; by **one** → autocracy/dictatorship; by **the mob** → mobocracy (or ochlocracy); **no government** → anarchy; **rule by a king/queen** → monarchy.

**Studies and -graphy words:** geography (earth's surface), demography (populations), cartography (maps), calligraphy (beautiful writing), hagiography (saints' lives), etymology (word origins), philology (language history). The stem 'study of ___' names the object; the -ology/-graphy suffix names the family.

**Speech and writing words** form their own tight set — prologue/epilogue (start/end of a literary work), epitaph (tomb inscription), elegy (mourning poem), eulogy (words of praise for the dead), euphemism (mild substitute for a harsh word), soliloquy (talking to oneself), extempore (unprepared). Two overlapping pairs are the classic traps: *elegy vs eulogy* (both about the dead: mourning vs praise) and *epitaph vs epilogue* (tomb vs play's end).

**Time and frequency words:** century (100 years), decade (10), annual (yearly), biennial (every two years), biannual (twice a year), diurnal (daily/by day), nocturnal (by night). The biannual/biennial pair decides itself: -ennial counts years, -annual counts per year.

**That-which-cannot-be set:** inevitable, incredible, invisible, inaudible, illegible, incorrigible, inexplicable — all 'in-/il- + verb of perception or action'. The stem names the verb ('read' → illegible), so link each to its verb: believe→incredible, see→invisible, hear→inaudible, read→illegible, avoid→inevitable, correct→incorrigible.

tricks.title: Ruler-first matching
tricks.body: Underline WHO rules in the stem (people, rich, officials, one, God) and match to democracy/plutocracy/bureaucracy/autocracy/theocracy. The stem hands you the answer's head word.

tricks.title: Verb-link the negatives
tricks.body: Chain each 'cannot-be' word to its verb: read→illegible, believe→incredible, see→invisible. Stems always quote the verb.

tricks.title: Dead-word precision
tricks.body: About the dead: praise → eulogy, mourning-poem → elegy, tomb-writing → epitaph. Three cards, three certain marks.

mistakes: Choosing 'astrology' for a scientific study of stars.
Swapping biannual (twice a year) and biennial (every two years).
Using 'elegy' where praise of the dead is asked (that is 'eulogy').
Confusing anarchy (no government) with autocracy (one ruler).

subtopics.title: Exam strategy for one-word substitution
subtopics.concept:
Tier 1 gives 1–2 OWS items; Tier 2 a few more. Like vocabulary, these are 15-second marks governed by recall — so the strategy is a *banking* strategy.

**Bank in categories, not lists.** One day: all -cide words. Next: fear words. Next: places. Categories cross-link (regicide joins reg- king with -cide killing), and cross-linked memories survive exam stress.

**Daily 10-minute rotation:** 10 new words + 20 old words read aloud. Weekend: 30-word mixed self-test. Every OWS word you meet in mocks goes into the personal sheet — repeats are frequent.

**In the exam:**
1. Read the stem and classify the family (killing? fear? study? person? place? group? government? cannot-be?).
2. Reject options from other families — usually two die here.
3. Match the stem's exact object (bees not birds; king not brother; praise not mourning).
4. If two options remain in-family, take the more specific one — OWS stems reward specificity (regicide beats homicide for 'murder of a king').

**Never leave it blank.** Even at 50-50 within a family, choose — no negative marking economics justify a skip on a recall item.

**Do not over-invest.** OWS is worth a couple of marks; the bank in this topic (150+ words) plus your mock sheet is sufficient. Beyond that, hours belong to RC and grammar.

tricks.title: Specificity rule
tricks.body: When two options fit the family, the stem's detail decides: 'brother' → fratricide, not homicide; 'twice a year' → biannual, not annual.

tricks.title: Stem-object underline
tricks.body: Underline the noun the word must carry (bees, grain, king, tomb). One underline removes half the options.

tricks.title: Mock-word ledger
tricks.body: Keep one running sheet titled 'OWS from mocks'. Most repeats come from your own past mistakes, not from unknown words.

mistakes: Reading the OWS bank once and expecting recall a month later.
Choosing a same-family but wrong-object word under time pressure.
Skipping the item when two options confuse, instead of applying specificity.
Spending entire revision days on OWS while grammar and RC — the real marks — wait.

pyqPatterns.approach: Anchor the object or trait (shoes, stars-scientific, overeats) and match; kill same-family neighbours by object.
Match suffix family first, then the root object (king→regicide, water→hydrophobia, insects→entomology).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Stems: 'A place where ___ is kept' / 'A group of ___'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Stored-object anchor for places; animal-first matching for groups; beware one-letter pairs (apiary/aviary).
Underline the ruler noun and map to democracy, plutocracy, bureaucracy, autocracy, theocracy, monarchy, anarchy.
Link the verb to its negative word: see→invisible, read→illegible, believe→incredible, avoid→inevitable.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Stems about speeches, tomb writings, mourning poems, unprepared talks.
pyqPatterns.approach: Keep the triple cards straight: praise→eulogy, mourning→elegy, tomb→epitaph; unprepared→extempore.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Murder of a king
solvedExamples.solution: The stem is a killing word (-cide family). Within the family, the object decides: rex/reg = king → **regicide**. *Homicide* is killing of a human in general, *genocide* of a race, *infanticide* of an infant — all real words planted as family-mates.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Family first (-cide), then the root object (rex = king).

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where bees are kept
solvedExamples.solution: Place stems are anchored by the stored object: bees → **apiary**. *Aviary* is the one-letter neighbour (birds), *aquarium* holds fish, *granary* grain.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Stored-object anchor: bees → apiary. Watch the aviary trap.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A medicine that counteracts poison
solvedExamples.solution: The anti- options form the family; the function decides: counteracts poison → **antidote**. *Antibiotic* kills bacteria, *antiseptic* prevents infection on wounds, *anaesthetic* removes sensation.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Function matching within the anti- family.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who loves books
practice.solution: Biblio = book + phile = lover → **bibliophile**. *Philatelist* collects stamps, *lexicographer* compiles dictionaries, *philanthropist* loves humankind through charity.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A person who talks in his sleep
practice.solution: Somni = sleep + loqui = speak → **somniloquist**. *Somnambulist* walks in sleep (ambul = walk) — the classic sibling trap; *insomniac* cannot sleep at all.
practice.shortcut: somni- (sleep) + verb root decides: walk vs speak.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Government by the people through their elected representatives
practice.solution: Demos = people + cracy = rule → **democracy**. The stem names the ruler ('the people'); the other options name one ruler, officials, and nobles respectively.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who can use both hands with equal ease
practice.solution: Ambi = both + dextr = right hand/skill → **ambidextrous**. *Ambivalent* means having mixed feelings, *amphibious* means living on land and water — the ambi-/amphi- family tempts, the dextr root decides.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where bees are kept
practice.solution: Bees are kept in an **apiary**; *aviary* (one letter away) keeps birds, *aquarium* fish, *granary* grain.
practice.shortcut: Stored-object anchor; the aviary trap is deliberate.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The act of killing one's own brother
practice.solution: Frater = brother → **fratricide**. *Patricide* kills the father, *regicide* the king, *genocide* a whole community — all -cide family-mates separated by the relation root.
practice.shortcut: Family root decides the relation: frater = brother.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A speech delivered without any preparation
practice.solution: Unprepared speech = **extempore**. *Epilogue* closes a play, *monologue* is a long one-person speech (prepared or not), *elocution* is the art of clear speaking.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who studies the stars and other heavenly bodies scientifically
practice.solution: The word 'scientifically' fixes **astronomer** — the scientist of the sky. *Astrologer* predicts fates from star positions; *cosmonaut* travels; *geologist* studies the earth.
practice.shortcut: Science vs prediction: astronomer vs astrologer — the stem's adjective decides.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

An abnormal fear of enclosed spaces
practice.solution: Claustro = enclosed → **claustrophobia**. The family: hydro- water, acro- heights, xeno- foreigners — the stem names the feared object and the suffix names the family.
practice.shortcut: phobia family; match the feared object.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Words inscribed on a tomb
practice.solution: Tomb inscription = **epitaph**. *Epilogue* ends a play, *elegy* mourns in verse, *epigram* is a witty short saying — the epi- family is planted wholesale.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A person appointed to hear both sides and settle a dispute
practice.solution: An **arbitrator** is the authorised settler of disputes. *Agitator* stirs trouble, *dictator* rules absolutely, *philanthropist* gives to charity — different families entirely.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of lions
practice.solution: Lions live in a **pride**. *Herd* suits cattle, *swarm* bees, *flock* sheep or birds — the four collective options are swapped around in every paper.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who is present everywhere at the same time
practice.solution: Omni = all + present → **omnipresent**. The omni-triplet: -potent (power), -scient (knowledge), -present (place) — the stem names the dimension.
practice.shortcut: Omni- family: match the ending to the stem's dimension (place → present).

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A medicine that counteracts the effects of poison
practice.solution: Counteracts poison = **antidote**. *Antibiotic* attacks bacteria, *antiseptic* prevents wound infection, *anaesthetic* kills sensation during surgery.
practice.shortcut: anti- family; function match: poison → antidote.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

That which cannot be avoided
practice.solution: Cannot be avoided = **inevitable**. Link each option to its verb: conquer→invincible, see→invisible, believe→incredible. The stem's verb ('avoided') picks its partner.
